title: Closing Costs Explained: What You're Actually Paying For
description: Closing costs aren't a mystery. Learn what each category covers, which costs you can shop for, and how to read your Loan Estimate with confidence.
image_alt: A person at a desk holding a small model house next to a calculator

faq.q: When will I find out my closing costs?
faq.a: Your lender must send a Loan Estimate within three business days of receiving your application, and a Closing Disclosure at least three business days before you close.

faq.q: Can the seller pay my closing costs?
faq.a: Often, yes. Seller credits are common and allowed within limits that depend on your loan program, your down payment, and how you'll use the property.

faq.q: Which closing costs can I shop for?
faq.a: Your Loan Estimate lists services you can shop for, which often include title services and the settlement agent. Lender fees and the appraisal are typically not shoppable.

body_html:
Most buyers spend months thinking about their down payment and about five minutes thinking about closing costs. Then the Loan Estimate arrives with two pages of line items, and the questions start: What's a recording fee? Why am I paying for title insurance? Why does my payment include money for taxes I haven't been billed for yet?

Closing costs aren't mysterious once you know how they're grouped. Here's the plain-English version I walk my clients through.

The three big buckets

Nearly every charge on your Loan Estimate falls into one of three groups.

  • Lender charges. What it costs to originate and process the loan, plus any points you choose to pay to adjust your rate.
  • Third-party services. The people and companies that make the transaction work: appraiser, credit report provider, title company, escrow or settlement agent, and sometimes a pest or home inspector.
  • Government fees and prepaids. Recording and transfer taxes charged by the county, plus money collected up front for homeowners insurance, property taxes, and interest from your closing date to the end of that month.

That last bucket surprises people the most. Prepaids aren't really a fee. They're your own future bills, collected early so your escrow account starts with a cushion.

Reading the Loan Estimate without a headache

The federal Loan Estimate form is standardized, which is good news: once you know where to look, you can compare offers line by line. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has an interactive guide to every section if you want to go deeper.

SectionWhat it coversCan you shop for it?
A. Origination chargesLender fees and any pointsCompare across lenders
B. Services you cannot shop forAppraisal, credit report, flood certificationNo
C. Services you can shop forTitle services, settlement agent, surveysYes
E. Taxes and other government feesRecording fees, transfer taxesNo
F and G. Prepaids and initial escrowInsurance, property taxes, interim interestPartly, through your insurance choice

Where the real savings usually hide

Buyers tend to fixate on the smallest fees. The meaningful differences are usually in a few places:

  • Points and credits. Paying points can lower your rate; taking a lender credit can lower your cash to close. The right trade depends on how long you expect to keep the loan.
  • Homeowners insurance. Premiums vary widely, especially in parts of California where insurance has become harder to place. Start shopping early.
  • Your closing date. Closing later in the month means less prepaid interest at the table. It doesn't change the total cost of the loan, but it can ease the cash you need that day.

Who pays what in a California purchase

Custom varies by county. In much of Southern California, buyers and sellers commonly split escrow fees, and who pays for the owner's title policy can depend on local practice and what's negotiated in the contract. Your agent will know what's typical where you're buying, and everything is negotiable.

Seller credits are one of the most useful tools here. Instead of a price reduction, a seller can contribute toward your closing costs. Each loan program caps how much, so check with your loan officer before writing it into an offer.

Three numbers to watch as you get closer

  1. Cash to close. Down payment plus closing costs, minus deposits and credits. This is the number you'll actually wire.
  2. Changes from Loan Estimate to Closing Disclosure. Federal rules limit how much certain fees can increase. If something moved, ask why.
  3. Your final monthly payment. Principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any mortgage insurance together. Budget for the full number, not just the loan payment.

One last tip: never wire funds based on an emailed instruction alone. Call your escrow officer at a number you already know is correct to confirm wiring details. Wire fraud targets home buyers every day.

Points and lender credits, explained simply

Discount points are an upfront payment that lowers your interest rate. Lender credits work in the opposite direction: you accept a slightly higher rate, and the lender pays some of your closing costs. Neither is better in general. The right choice depends on how long you'll keep the loan.

If you expect to stay in the home and keep the loan for many years, paying points can make sense because the monthly savings add up. If you might sell or refinance in a few years, a lender credit that keeps your cash in your pocket may be the smarter move. Ask your loan officer to show both versions side by side so you can see the break-even point.

The takeaway

Closing costs aren't a black box. They're a list of real services, government charges, and your own prepaid bills. Read your Loan Estimate section by section, focus on the items that actually move, and ask questions early. If you want a second set of eyes on a Loan Estimate, even one from another lender, I'm happy to walk through it with you. It also helps to start with a solid pre-approval so there are no surprises later.
